'''''Asparagopsis armata''''' is a species of marine red algae, in the family [[Bonnemaisoniaceae]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Zanolla|first=M.|date=2015|title=Photosynthetic Plasticity of the Genus Asparagopsis (Bonnemaisoniales, Rhodophyta) in Response to Temperature: Implications for Invasiveness|journal=Biological Invasions|volume=17|issue=5|pages=1341–1353|doi=10.1007/s10530-014-0797-8|bibcode=2015BiInv..17.1341Z |s2cid=18279567|hdl=10630/33478|hdl-access=free}}</ref> English name(s) include '''red harpoon weed'''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=MarLIN - The Marine Life Information Network - Harpoon weed (Asparagopsis armata) |url=https://www.marlin.ac.uk/species/detail/1619 |access-date=2022-07-01 |website=www.marlin.ac.uk |language=en-GB}}</ref> They are [[multicellular]] [[eukaryotic]] organisms. This species was first described in 1855 by Harvey,<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Andreakis|first1=Nikos|last2=Procaccini|first2=Gabriele|last3=Kooistra|first3=Wiebe HCF|date=2004-08-01|title=Asparagopsis taxiformis and Asparagopsis armata (Bonnemaisoniales, Rhodophyta): genetic and morphological identification of Mediterranean populations|url=https://doi.org/10.1080/0967026042000236436|journal=European Journal of Phycology|volume=39|issue=3|pages=273–283|doi=10.1080/0967026042000236436|bibcode=2004EJPhy..39..273A |s2cid=84044248|issn=0967-0262|url-access=subscription}}</ref> an Irish botanist who found the algae on the Western Australian coast. ''A. armata'' usually develops on infralittoral rocky bottoms around the seawater surface to around 40m of depth. Marine algae like ''A. armata'' are considered "autogenic ecosystem engineers" as they are at the very bottom of the food chain and control resource availability to other organisms in the ecosystem.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Crooks|first=J.A.|date=2002|title=Characterizing ecosystem-level consequences of Biological Invasions, the role of ecosystem engineers|journal=Oikos|volume=97|issue=2|pages=153–166|doi=10.1034/j.1600-0706.2002.970201.x|bibcode=2002Oikos..97..153C }}</ref>

== Population distribution ==
''A. armata'' is a species native to [[southern Australia]] and [[New Zealand]] ([[Southern Hemisphere|Southern hemisphere]]) and is thought to have slowly spread to the Northern hemisphere through the Mediterranean sea, as it is highly invasive. It can now also be found along the [[British Isles]] to [[Senegal]] as well.<ref>{{Cite book|first1=P.S. |last1=Dixon |first2=L.M. |last2=Irvine |title=Seaweeds of the British Isles : Vol. 1: Rhodophyta Part 1: Introduction, Nemaliales, Gigartinales|date=1977|publisher=British Museum|isbn=0-565-00781-5|oclc=769250096}}</ref> The first Mediterranean ''A. armata'' was reported in Algeria in 1923. When first found, it was considered abnormal to find ''A. armata'' in this location due to the high summer seawater surface temperatures along southern [[Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]] coasts. However, it was later found that the particular cool water temperatures that stay below 25 °C would allow the species to survive locally during the summer.<ref name=":0" />

== Morphology ==
The fully grown ''A. armata'' has sparse branches on which long [[Stolon|stolons]] with harpoon-like hooks and erect shoots develop in all directions. The branches, stolons, and shoots ramify over and over again which give ''A. armata'' the thallus-like appearance.<ref name=":0" /> The ultimate branchlets are filamentous and composed of three cell rows whereas the larger branches consist of a central medullary filament and a gelatinous matrix surrounded by a cortex 3 – 6 cells thick.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Børgesen|first=Frederik|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.1314|title=The marine Algæ of the Danish West Indies.|date=1913|publisher=Printed by B. Luno|location=Copenhagen|doi=10.5962/bhl.title.1314}}</ref> [[Gametophyte|Gametophytes]] are [[terete]] and are around 200 mm in height. They form dense, pink intertwining clumps. A characteristic feature of this species is barbs, which attach the ''A. armata'' to the ocean benthic substrates.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Asparagopsis armata - Invasive Alien Species Fact Sheet for Mediterranean Network of MPAs|url=http://www.iucn-medmis.org/srv/species/pdf/2?language=en|website=Online Database MedMIS IUCN Center for Mediterranean Cooperation}}</ref>

== Life cycle ==
''A. armata'' has a triphasic diplohaplontic heteromorphic life cycle. In this cycle, the three phases include: haploid carposporophyte, gametophyte and diploid zygote. Multiple phases of different [[Morphology (biology)|morphology]] and [[ploidy]] contribute differently to the expansion potential of ''A. armata''. Gametophytes of this species are microscopic carposoporophytes, which divide into tetrasporophytes that go through meiosis to be developed into the gametophyte.

''A. armata'' has two morphologically different stages of development– the [[gametophyte]] stage and the tetrasporophyte stage. 
[[File:Life cycle of A. armata.png|thumb]]
''A. armata'' goes through haploid and gametophytic phases in a [[Self-incompatibility|heteromorphic]] diplo-haplontic life cycle.<ref name=":0" /> The ''A. armata'' gametophyte grows into adult form and goes through fecundation to produce diploid carposporophyte; which, then, divide into [[Tetrasporaphyte|tetrasporophyte]] that goes through [[meiosis]] to be developed into the [[gametophyte]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Guiry|first1=Michael D.|last2=Dawes|first2=Clinton J.|date=1992-06-25|title=Daylength, temperature and nutrient control of tetrasporogenesis in Asparagopsis armata (Rhodophyta)|url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016%2F0022-0981%2892%2990227-2|journal=Journal of Experimental Marine Biology and Ecology|language=en|volume=158|issue=2|pages=197–217|doi=10.1016/0022-0981(92)90227-2|bibcode=1992JEMBE.158..197G |issn=0022-0981|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Impact of ''A. armata'' as an invasive species ==
The acceleration of marine biological invasions through increasing trade and travel also caused the transportation of ''A. armata'' to areas outside of their native range in the Southern hemisphere. Once it is established, ''A. armata'' could rapidly spread and dominate the [[Invasive species|invaded environment]] without the direct intervention of human activity.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Fifty years of invasion ecology : the legacy of Charles Elton|date=2011|publisher=Wiley-Blackwell|first=D. M.|last=Richardson|isbn=978-1-4443-3585-9|location=Chichester, West Sussex|oclc=652743661}}</ref> ''A. armata'' releases large amounts of toxic compounds to gain competitive advantage in the surrounding invaded area.<ref name=":1">{{cite journal | doi=10.3390/toxins13010015 | doi-access=free | title=Impacts of the Invasive Seaweed Asparagopsis armata Exudate on Energetic Metabolism of Rock Pool Invertebrates | date=2020 | last1=Silva | first1=Carla | last2=Novais | first2=Sara | last3=Soares | first3=Amadeu | last4=Barata | first4=Carlos | last5=Lemos | first5=Marco | journal=Toxins | volume=13 | issue=1 | page=15 | pmid=33375546 | pmc=7823594 }}</ref> The impairment of invertebrates after exposure to this algal exudate is shown by significantly increased lipid  (and other biochemical biomarkers) content in the organisms such as common prawn and [[Sea snail|marine snail]].<ref name=":1" /> The critical impact that the exudate of ''A. armata'' causes, via secondary metabolites, severely decreases the survival rate of various species in the rock pool native communities.<ref name=":1" />

== Halogenated metabolites ==
As a defense mechanism against its predators, ''A. armata'' produce [[Halogenation|halogenated]] metabolites that chase away herbivores and prevent biofouling. These halogenated metabolites are stored as a refractile inclusion inside specialized gland cells, and are activated with [[Bromine]].

Gland cells of ''A. armata'' can take up to 10% of the algal volume, which is a large portion of the plant. Gland cell walls are thin in order to help the transfer of metabolites to the structures that connect the gland cells to the pericentral cells. These structures are stalk-like and allow the metabolite to move to the algae's surface.
<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Paul|first1=Nicholas A.|last2=Cole|first2=Louise|last3=Nys|first3=Rocky De|last4=Steinberg|first4=Peter D.|date=2006|title=Ultrastructure of the Gland Cells of the Red Alga Asparagopsis Armata (bonnemaisoniaceae)1|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1529-8817.2006.00226.x|journal=Journal of Phycology|language=en|volume=42|issue=3|pages=637–645|doi=10.1111/j.1529-8817.2006.00226.x|bibcode=2006JPcgy..42..637P |s2cid=85291068|issn=1529-8817|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Methane emissions reduction in ruminants ==
In 2019, following laboratory studies on the effectiveness of ''[[Asparagopsis taxiformis]]'' in reducing ruminants' enteric methane emissions, a team from the [[University of California, Davis]], demonstrated that a 1% inclusion of ''Asparagopsis armata'' in lactating dairy cows' feed resulted in a 67.2% decrease in methane produced.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Roque |first1=Breanna M. |last2=Salwen |first2=Joan K. |last3=Kinley |first3=Rob |last4=Kebreab |first4=Ermias |date=October 10, 2019 |title=Inclusion of Asparagopsis armata in lactating dairy cows' diet reduces enteric methane emission by over 50 percent |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0959652619321559 |journal=Journal of Cleaner Production |volume=234 |pages=132–138 |doi=10.1016/j.jclepro.2019.06.193 |bibcode=2019JCPro.234..132R |s2cid=197795543 |via=Elsevier Science Direct|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In 2021, {{Proper name|CH4 Global}} became the first company in the world to be licensed by intellectual property holders [[FutureFeed]] to use Asparagopsis in livestock feed, with the aim of significantly reducing enteric methane emissions in ruminants. These licences enable {{Proper name|CH4 Global}} to make methane reduction claims about the Asparagopsis in their product formulations in the New Zealand and Australian markets,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Using seaweed to reduce livestock emissions and mitigate climate change |url=https://minterellison.staging.beingbui.lt/our-view/using-seaweed-to-reduce-livestock-emissions-and-mitigate-climate-change |access-date=2022-12-05 |website=minterellison.staging.beingbui.lt}}</ref> where the company has research and production facilities. ''A. armata'' is the dominant species of Asparagopsis in New Zealand.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bonin |first1=Denise R. |last2=Hawkes |first2=Michael W. |date=October 1987 |title=Systematics and life histories of New Zealand Bonnemaisoniaceae (Bonnemaisoniales, Rhodophyta): I. The genus Asparagopsis |journal=New Zealand Journal of Botany |language=en |volume=25 |issue=4 |pages=577–590 |doi=10.1080/0028825X.1987.10410088 |issn=0028-825X|doi-access=free |bibcode=1987NZJB...25..577B }}</ref> {{Proper name|CH4 Global}} worked with New Zealand's [[National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research|National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research (NIWA)]] to close the life cycle of the seaweed, which they accomplished in June of the same year,<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 4, 2021 |title=Research Collaboration Uncovers Mechanisms To Trigger Spore Release For Asparagopsis Seaweed {{!}} Scoop News |url=https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/SC2106/S00010/research-collaboration-uncovers-mechanisms-to-trigger-spore-release-for-asparagopsis-seaweed.htm |access-date=2022-12-05 |website=www.scoop.co.nz}}</ref> enabling large quantities of the seaweed to be aquafarmed. CH4 Global has since pulled out of New Zealand and is operating in Australia. Asparagopsis Technologies <ref>{{Cite web |title=Asparagopsis Technologies |url=https://asparagopsis.co/ |access-date=2026-08-11 |language=en-US}}</ref> is now operating out of the site in Ocean Beach, Bluff which was previously built and operated by CH4 global. 

Sea Forest, based in Tasmania, Australia, and also a [[FutureFeed]] licensee, has chosen to focus exclusively on ''A. armata'', and has worked with scientists at [[James Cook University]], [[University of Tasmania]], [[University of Technology Sydney]], and [[University of New South Wales]] in Australia, and the [[University of Waikato]] in New Zealand, to find out how to trigger its reproduction.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hughes |first=Lesley |date=2022-09-02 |title=From designing clothes to refashioning cow burps: Sam's $40 million career switch |url=https://www.smh.com.au/national/from-designing-clothes-to-refashioning-cow-burps-sam-s-40-million-career-switch-20220719-p5b2pn.html |access-date=2022-12-05 |website=The Sydney Morning Herald |language=en}}</ref>
